transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad you're here today. What brings you in to see me?

Over the last month I’ve just lost interest in my art, dancing, and even my job, and I can’t seem to care about anything the way I used to. It's really hard because I usually love those things, but now everything just feels completely flat.
Have you experienced any major life changes, stressors, or difficult events recently around the time these feelings started?

Yes, it started during a really stressful tax season at my accounting firm; we were short-staffed, so I took on a ton of extra accounts to prove I was ready for CPA coursework. For a few weeks I rode this huge wave of intense energy and productivity, but once the rush ended, I just completely crashed into this flat, heavy state.
During that period of high energy, did you find that you needed much less sleep than usual but still felt fully rested and active?

Yes, during those weeks I was only sleeping about three or four hours a night but would wake up feeling completely energized. I didn't feel tired at all, and it honestly felt like sleep was just getting in the way of all my projects.
During that high-energy period, did you feel like your thoughts were racing or moving so fast that it was hard to keep up with them?

Yes, my thoughts were definitely racing and felt like they were all firing at once. I was constantly jumping between ideas for helping local Latino business owners, tweaking our billing process, and planning art projects, and I just couldn't slow down enough to focus on one thing.
During that high-energy period, did you find yourself engaging in impulsive or risky behaviors, such as spending too much money or making reckless decisions?

No, I don't really recall doing anything reckless or spending excessive money during that time. I was mostly just incredibly busy, focusing all my energy on my accounting work and planning ideas for my side bookkeeping business.
During that high-energy period, did your family, friends, or coworkers notice a change in your behavior or comment on how differently you were acting?

Yes, my coworkers definitely noticed and actually joked that I’d had way too much coffee. They said I was talking a mile a minute, jumping from one business idea to the next without really letting anyone else get a word in.
How has this flat, heavy feeling affected your ability to manage your daily work and personal life, and have you experienced any thoughts of self-harm or suicide?

It’s really messed things up—I’ve had to have meetings with my supervisor about mistakes I'm suddenly making at work, I've stopped going to my salsa classes, and my dishes and laundry are just piling up at home. But to answer your other question, I definitely haven't had any thoughts of self-harm or suicide.
Have you ever had a period of high energy, similar to the one you described, that was so intense it caused major problems in your life, led to reckless decisions, or required hospitalization?

No, it never caused major problems or led to anything like hospitalization. I just felt incredibly buzzed, productive, and fast-paced, even if my coworkers thought I was talking too fast or being a bit snappy when they couldn't keep up.
Since you started feeling this flat and heavy over the past month, have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns, appetite, or physical energy levels?

Yes, my sleep is awful now; I toss and turn for hours and wake up at three in the morning worrying about work mistakes, feeling like I never really slept. I also have no appetite and have to force myself to eat even half a sandwich, so my clothes are starting to get loose. My body just feels incredibly heavy and I'm dragging myself around completely exhausted all day.

During any of your high-energy periods, did you ever feel like you had special powers, supreme authority, or a unique connection to a higher power, or did you ever hear or see things that others couldn't?

No, nothing like that—I've never heard or seen things, or felt like I had special powers. But I did have this really intense, unrealistic confidence where I truly believed I was the only one in the office who understood our clients' finances and could easily start my own firm, even though I hadn't even started my CPA classes yet.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a current major depressive episode lasting one month, characterized by depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, decreased appetite with weight loss, and fatigue, resulting in significant functional impairment. This was immediately preceded by a distinct period of hypomania lasting several weeks, characterized by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, pressured speech, increased goal-directed activity, and inflated self-esteem (grandiosity). This episode did not cause severe impairment, require hospitalization, or feature psychotic symptoms, ruling out a manic episode. The combination of at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode confirms the diagnosis of Bipolar II disorder (F31.8).
